passages.title: The opening claim becomes an invitation to come and see
passages.summary: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God and was God. All things were made through him. The Word became flesh and lived among us. John the Baptist says he is not the Christ. He points to Jesus as the Lamb of God. Two of John’s disciples follow Jesus and spend the day with him. Andrew brings his brother Simon. Philip brings Nathanael, who doubts that anything good comes from Nazareth.

lds.text: The selected lesson studies light and inviting others to come and see. Why does John direct his own followers toward another person?

contextNote.title: The opening claim becomes an invitation to come and see
contextNote.text: The chapter opens with the largest claims in the book. It then turns to a simple scene. Two men ask Jesus where he is staying (verse 38). Verse 39 answers, “Come and see.” They go and stay the day. Philip uses the same words to Nathanael in verse 46. The great claim is offered as an invitation to look.

passages.title: Remembering after resurrection changes understanding of the temple saying
passages.summary: Jesus and his disciples attend a wedding at Cana. The wine runs out, and his mother tells him. He has six stone jars filled with water. The water becomes fine wine, and his disciples believe in him. He goes up to Jerusalem for the Passover. He drives the sellers and money changers out of the temple. He says, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.” He was speaking about his body.

lds.text: The selected lesson studies the wedding sign and care for sacred places. How does later remembrance change the meaning of the temple saying?

contextNote.title: Remembering after resurrection changes understanding of the temple saying
contextNote.text: The hearers think Jesus means the building (verse 20). Verse 21 says he meant his body. No one understood at the time, including the disciples. Verse 22 says they remembered after he was raised. Then they believed the Scripture and his word. John tells the story from that later point of view. Some sayings can be understood only after the events they point to.

passages.title: A teacher's questions stand beside a witness's willingness to decrease
passages.summary: Nicodemus, a Pharisee and ruler, comes to Jesus at night. Jesus says no one can see God’s Kingdom without being born anew. Nicodemus asks how that can be. Jesus says God loved the world and gave his only Son. Light has come, and people loved darkness. John’s disciples complain that everyone is going to Jesus. John says he is the bridegroom’s friend and is glad. He says Jesus must increase and he must decrease.

lds.text: The selected lesson teaches spiritual rebirth through Christ. How does John’s bridegroom comparison answer his disciples’ concern about losing followers?

contextNote.title: A teacher's questions stand beside a witness's willingness to decrease
contextNote.text: John’s disciples are worried about losing their following (verse 26). John answers with a wedding. The bride belongs to the bridegroom (verse 29). The friend stands by and is glad to hear the groom’s voice. John says his joy is complete. Verse 30 then states his place in one line. He was sent to point to another, so growing smaller is success.

passages.title: The woman's invitation leads others to hear for themselves
passages.summary: Jesus travels through Samaria and rests at Jacob’s well. He asks a Samaritan woman for a drink. He offers her living water and tells her about her life. She asks where people ought to worship. He says true worshipers worship in spirit and truth. She tells her town to come and see. Many Samaritans believe and ask him to stay. In Galilee he heals an official’s son with a word.

lds.text: The selected lesson reads living water through spiritual needs and growing testimony. How does the town’s own hearing develop the woman’s invitation?

contextNote.title: The woman's invitation leads others to hear for themselves
contextNote.text: The woman leaves her water jar and goes to the town (verse 28). She says, “Come, see a man” (verse 29). Many believe because of her word (verse 39). They ask Jesus to stay, and he stays two days. Verse 42 reports what they then tell her. They now believe because they have heard for themselves. Her invitation did its work by bringing them to him.

passages.title: The man's lack of help leads into a dispute about work
passages.summary: In Jerusalem many sick people lie beside a pool. One man has been ill for thirty-eight years. Jesus asks whether he wants to be well. The man says he has no one to put him in the water. Jesus tells him to take up his mat and walk. It is the Sabbath, and the leaders object. Jesus says his Father is working and he is working. He says the Scriptures testify about him.
passages.uncertainty: Selected markers distinguish events from quoted origins and remembered places. Bethany beyond the Jordan is separate from Bethany near Jerusalem. Exact gardens, pools, houses, and routes remain unassigned.

lds.text: Doctrine and Covenants 76:15–18 says a vision followed study of verse 29. What prevents the man from reaching the water before Jesus speaks?

contextNote.title: The man's lack of help leads into a dispute about work
contextNote.text: Jesus asks the man a direct question in verse 6. The man does not say yes. Verse 7 explains why he has not been healed. He has no one to help him into the pool. Others always get there first. He has been alone among a crowd for years. Jesus heals him with a word, and the dispute turns to Sabbath work.

passages.title: A meal leads to words that some followers cannot accept
passages.summary: Jesus feeds five thousand with five barley loaves and two fish. The crowd wants to make him king, and he withdraws. He walks on the sea to his disciples. The crowd finds him and asks for more bread. He says he is the bread of life that came down from heaven. He speaks of eating his flesh and drinking his blood. Many disciples call this a hard saying and leave. Peter says there is no one else to go to.
passages.uncertainty: Selected markers distinguish events from quoted origins and remembered places. Bethany beyond the Jordan is separate from Bethany near Jerusalem. Exact gardens, pools, houses, and routes remain unassigned.

lds.text: Why does Peter remain when other disciples leave after the same teaching?

contextNote.title: A meal leads to words that some followers cannot accept
contextNote.text: Verse 60 says many disciples found the teaching hard. Verse 66 says they left and walked with him no more. Jesus asks the twelve whether they will leave too. Peter does not say he understands. Verse 68 asks where else they would go. He stays because of who Jesus is and what he has found in his words. Verse 69 adds that they have come to believe and know.

passages.title: The divided crowd prevents a single response from representing everyone
passages.summary: Jesus’s brothers urge him to show himself at the Feast of Booths. He goes up in secret and then teaches in the temple. Some say he is a good man, and others say he deceives the people. Officers are sent to arrest him. On the last day he invites the thirsty to come and drink. The crowd is divided over him. The officers return without him and say no one ever spoke like this. Nicodemus asks whether the law judges a man unheard.

lds.text: How does Nicodemus’ hearing request challenge the proposed judgment?

contextNote.title: The divided crowd prevents a single response from representing everyone
contextNote.text: This chapter shows a crowd that cannot agree. Verses 12, 40–43 record several opinions at once. The rulers want an arrest and scorn the crowd (verse 49). Nicodemus is one of those rulers. Verse 51 asks a plain legal question. Does their law condemn a man before hearing him? No single response in the chapter speaks for everyone.

passages.title: Claims about ancestry meet the question of present conduct
passages.summary: Jesus says he is the light of the world. The Pharisees say his witness about himself is not valid. He tells those who believed him that the truth will set them free. They answer that they are Abraham’s children and were never slaves. He says everyone who sins is a slave to sin. If they were Abraham’s children, they would do what Abraham did. They are trying to kill him. He says, “Before Abraham came into existence, I AM.”
passages.uncertainty: Selected markers distinguish events from quoted origins and remembered places. Bethany beyond the Jordan is separate from Bethany near Jerusalem. Exact gardens, pools, houses, and routes remain unassigned.

lds.text: How does claimed ancestry differ from the conduct Jesus names?

contextNote.title: Claims about ancestry meet the question of present conduct
contextNote.text: The hearers rest their case on ancestry (verses 33 and 39). Jesus does not deny their descent (verse 37). He asks what they are doing now. Verse 40 says they seek to kill a man who told them the truth. He adds, “Abraham didn’t do this.” A family line is shown by family likeness. The words belong to one heated dispute and should not be turned against a people.

passages.title: Repeated questioning gives the healed man a voice of his own
passages.summary: Jesus sees a man blind from birth. The disciples ask whose sin caused it. He says neither, and he heals the man with mud and washing. Neighbors and Pharisees question the man again and again. His parents are afraid and say he can speak for himself. He says he knows one thing: he was blind and now sees. They throw him out. Jesus finds him, and the man worships him.

lds.text: What remains consistent in the man’s answers as the questions repeat?

contextNote.title: Repeated questioning gives the healed man a voice of his own
contextNote.text: The man is questioned four times in this chapter. Each time he says a little more. He calls Jesus “the man” (verse 11) and then “a prophet” (verse 17). Verse 25 refuses to go beyond what he knows. He was blind, and now he sees. He will not call Jesus a sinner to please his judges. By verse 38 he says, “Lord, I believe.”

passages.title: The shepherd's care answers the danger of abandonment
passages.summary: Jesus says the shepherd enters by the door and the sheep know his voice. A thief comes only to steal and kill. Jesus says he is the door and the good shepherd. A hired man runs when the wolf comes. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep. He has other sheep that are not of this fold. At a winter feast some ask whether he is the Christ. He says, “I and the Father are one,” and they pick up stones.

lds.text: In 3 Nephi 15:21 Jesus calls a Book of Mormon people his “other sheep.” What distinguishes the shepherd from the hired worker when danger comes?

contextNote.title: The shepherd's care answers the danger of abandonment
contextNote.text: Verse 11 defines the good shepherd by one act. He lays down his life for the sheep. Verses 12–13 describe the hired man by contrast. He sees the wolf, leaves the flock, and runs. The sheep are not his, and he does not care about them. The test comes when danger arrives. Verse 18 adds that Jesus lays down his life of his own will.

passages.title: Restored life produces a plan for another death
passages.summary: Lazarus of Bethany falls ill, and his sisters send for Jesus. Jesus arrives after Lazarus has been dead four days. Martha says she believes he is the Christ. Jesus weeps at the tomb. He calls Lazarus out, and the dead man comes out wrapped in cloths. Many believe, and some report it to the Pharisees. The council fears that Rome will destroy their place and nation. The high priest says one man should die for the people.

lds.text: How does restored life become a reason for the council’s death plan?

contextNote.title: Restored life produces a plan for another death
contextNote.text: A man has been raised, and many believe (verse 45). The council treats that as a danger. Verse 48 gives their fear: Rome may take away their place and nation. Verse 50 gives the high priest’s reasoning. One death is better than the loss of all. Verses 51–52 say he spoke more truly than he knew. A gift of life leads directly to a plan for death (verse 53).

passages.title: The seed image changes the meaning of royal praise
passages.summary: Mary anoints Jesus’s feet with costly perfume, and Judas objects. A crowd welcomes Jesus to Jerusalem with palm branches. Some Greeks ask to see him. He says the hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified. A grain of wheat must fall into the earth and die to bear fruit. A voice from heaven answers him. He says that when he is lifted up he will draw all people to himself. Many still do not believe.
passages.uncertainty: Selected markers distinguish events from quoted origins and remembered places. Bethany beyond the Jordan is separate from Bethany near Jerusalem. Exact gardens, pools, houses, and routes remain unassigned.

lds.text: How does the dying seed change expectations about the announced hour?

contextNote.title: The seed image changes the meaning of royal praise
contextNote.text: The crowd has just hailed Jesus as king (verse 13). Foreigners are asking for him (verse 21). He says the hour of glory has come (verse 23). Verse 24 then explains what that glory is. A seed stays alone unless it is buried and dies. Only then does it bear much fruit. The praise at the gate is to be read through that picture.

passages.title: The teacher's lowered position supplies the example for followers
passages.summary: Before the Passover Jesus rises from supper and ties a towel around himself. He washes his disciples’ feet. Peter objects and then asks to be washed all over. Jesus says they should wash one another’s feet. He is troubled and says one of them will betray him. Judas takes the bread and goes out into the night. Jesus gives a new commandment: love one another as he has loved them. He tells Peter that he will deny him three times.
passages.uncertainty: This chapter has no selected place markers. Speech images do not establish an exact teaching location.

lds.text: Why does Jesus keep the titles Teacher and Lord while washing feet?

contextNote.title: The teacher's lowered position supplies the example for followers
contextNote.text: Verse 3 says Jesus knew the Father had given all things into his hands. With that knowledge he takes a servant’s towel. In verse 13 he accepts the titles Teacher and Lord. Verse 14 argues from them. If the Lord has washed their feet, they must wash each other’s. He does not give up his rank to serve. He shows what that rank is for.

passages.title: Questions about departure meet a promise of continued teaching
passages.summary: Jesus tells his disciples not to be troubled. He is going to prepare a place for them. Thomas says they do not know the way. Jesus says he is the way, the truth, and the life. Philip asks to see the Father. Jesus says whoever has seen him has seen the Father. He promises another Counselor, the Spirit of truth. He leaves them his peace.
passages.uncertainty: This chapter has no selected place markers. Speech images do not establish an exact teaching location.

lds.text: The selected lesson teaches the Holy Spirit’s help through teaching and remembrance. How will remembered words connect the promised Spirit with Jesus’ earlier teaching?

contextNote.title: Questions about departure meet a promise of continued teaching
contextNote.text: The disciples ask three anxious questions in this chapter (verses 5, 8, 22). They fear losing him. Verse 26 promises that his teaching will continue. The Holy Spirit will teach them and remind them of his words. The Spirit’s work is tied to what Jesus has already said. Their remembering will be helped. Verse 27 follows with a gift of peace.

passages.title: The vine image leads into the command to love
passages.summary: Jesus says he is the true vine and his Father is the gardener. Branches that bear fruit are pruned to bear more. A branch cannot bear fruit unless it remains in the vine. His disciples must remain in his love. His commandment is that they love one another as he loved them. He calls them friends and not servants. The world will hate them as it hated him. The Spirit and the disciples will bear witness.
passages.uncertainty: This chapter has no selected place markers. Speech images do not establish an exact teaching location.

lds.text: The selected lesson connects remaining in Christ with fruit and joy. Why does the branch need to remain joined even when it already bears fruit?

contextNote.title: The vine image leads into the command to love
contextNote.text: Verses 1–8 speak of branches and fruit. Verses 9–10 say that remaining in the vine means remaining in his love. Verse 12 then says what the fruit is. They are to love one another as he has loved them. Verse 13 measures that love by laying down one’s life. Verse 17 repeats the command. The picture of the vine leads straight to it.

passages.title: Confidence about understanding meets a warning of scattering
passages.summary: Jesus warns that his disciples will be put out of the synagogues. He says it is better for them that he goes away. The Counselor will come and guide them into all truth. They will weep, and their sorrow will turn to joy. He tells them to ask the Father in his name. The disciples say that now they understand and believe. He answers that they will soon be scattered and leave him alone. He tells them to take courage, for he has overcome the world.
passages.uncertainty: This chapter has no selected place markers. Speech images do not establish an exact teaching location.

lds.text: The selected lesson teaches guidance from the Holy Spirit. How does the scattering warning qualify the disciples’ new confidence?

contextNote.title: Confidence about understanding meets a warning of scattering
contextNote.text: In verses 29–30 the disciples say they finally understand. They are sure of their belief. Verse 31 answers with a question: “Do you now believe?” Verse 32 says they are about to scatter, each to his own home. They will leave him alone. Their confidence is real and not yet tested. Verse 33 gives them peace that rests on him, not on their firmness.

passages.title: The prayer extends belonging beyond the people presently listening
passages.summary: Jesus lifts his eyes to heaven and prays. He asks the Father to glorify the Son. He says eternal life is to know the only true God and Jesus Christ. He prays for those the Father gave him. He does not ask that they be taken out of the world. He asks that they be kept from the evil one. He prays also for those who will believe through their word. He asks that they all may be one.
passages.uncertainty: This chapter has no selected place markers. Speech images do not establish an exact teaching location.

lds.text: The selected lesson studies unity with the Father and among followers. Why does protection leave the followers within the world rather than remove them?

contextNote.title: The prayer extends belonging beyond the people presently listening
contextNote.text: Verses 6–19 pray for the disciples in the room. Verse 20 widens the prayer. It includes all who will believe through their word. Later readers are among those prayed for. Verse 21 asks that they all be one, as the Father and Son are one. The purpose is that the world may believe. Verse 15 says they stay in the world for that reason.

passages.title: Open testimony contrasts with denial and armed force
passages.summary: Jesus goes to a garden across the Kidron, and Judas brings soldiers. Jesus steps forward and says, “I am he.” Peter cuts off a servant’s ear, and Jesus tells him to put away his sword. Jesus is taken to the high priest. Peter denies him three times by a fire. Jesus tells the high priest that he taught openly. He is brought to Pilate, who asks whether he is a king. Jesus says his Kingdom is not of this world.

lds.text: How does Jesus’ answer about fighting explain his kingdom to Pilate?

contextNote.title: Open testimony contrasts with denial and armed force
contextNote.text: Pilate needs to know whether Jesus is a rival to Rome. Verse 36 answers by pointing to what his followers did not do. If his Kingdom were of this world, they would fight. Jesus stopped the one sword drawn for him (verse 11). His rule does not come by force. He has also said that he spoke openly (verse 20). Peter, meanwhile, denies him in the dark (verses 17, 25–27).

passages.title: The execution scene joins completed work with care for those remaining
passages.summary: Pilate has Jesus flogged, and soldiers crown him with thorns. Pilate says he finds no guilt and brings him out to the crowd. He hands him over to be crucified. The sign on the cross reads “Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews.” Soldiers divide his clothes. Jesus entrusts his mother to the disciple he loves. He says, “It is finished,” and dies. Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus bury him in a garden tomb.
passages.uncertainty: Selected markers distinguish events from quoted origins and remembered places. Bethany beyond the Jordan is separate from Bethany near Jerusalem. Exact gardens, pools, houses, and routes remain unassigned.

lds.text: How does care for his mother stand beside the statement of completed work?

contextNote.title: The execution scene joins completed work with care for those remaining
contextNote.text: Four soldiers are dividing his clothes (verses 23–24). Near the cross stand his mother and the disciple he loves. Verse 26 gives her a son, and verse 27 gives him a mother. From that hour the disciple takes her into his home. Jesus arranges her care while he is dying. Verse 30 then records, “It is finished.” The finished work includes this act for those left behind.

passages.title: Different paths to recognition lead toward readers who have not seen
passages.summary: Mary Magdalene finds the tomb open and runs to Peter and another disciple. They see the grave cloths and go home. Mary stays weeping and meets Jesus, whom she takes for the gardener. He says her name, and she knows him. That evening he appears to the disciples behind locked doors. Thomas is absent and says he will not believe without touching the wounds. A week later Jesus invites him to touch. John says he wrote so that readers may believe.
passages.uncertainty: Selected markers distinguish events from quoted origins and remembered places. Bethany beyond the Jordan is separate from Bethany near Jerusalem. Exact gardens, pools, houses, and routes remain unassigned.

lds.text: The selected lesson teaches resurrection through the Gospel accounts. How does the account’s stated purpose address readers who have not seen these signs?

contextNote.title: Different paths to recognition lead toward readers who have not seen
contextNote.text: People come to recognize Jesus in different ways in this chapter. One disciple sees the cloths and believes (verse 8). Mary knows him when he speaks her name (verse 16). Thomas asks to touch and then confesses him as Lord and God (verse 28). Verse 29 blesses those who have not seen. Verse 31 says the book was written for them. The written signs are offered to readers in place of sight.

passages.title: Peter's restored task does not determine another disciple's future
passages.summary: Seven disciples go fishing on the Sea of Tiberias and catch nothing. At dawn a man on the shore tells them to cast on the right side. The net fills, and they know it is the Lord. He gives them bread and fish beside a charcoal fire. He asks Peter three times whether he loves him. Each time he tells him to feed his sheep. Peter asks what will happen to another disciple. Jesus says that is not Peter’s concern.
passages.uncertainty: Selected markers distinguish events from quoted origins and remembered places. Bethany beyond the Jordan is separate from Bethany near Jerusalem. Exact gardens, pools, houses, and routes remain unassigned.

lds.text: The selected lesson connects love for Christ with feeding his sheep. How does the final correction distinguish a conditional saying from a certain prediction?

contextNote.title: Peter's restored task does not determine another disciple's future
contextNote.text: Peter denied Jesus three times beside a charcoal fire (18:18). Here he is asked three times beside another (verse 9). He receives a task and word of his own death (verses 18–19). Then he asks about another disciple (verse 21). Jesus says that is not Peter’s concern and tells him to follow. Verse 23 corrects a rumor that grew from this. Jesus said “if,” and people heard a promise.

events.title: Remembering after resurrection changes understanding of the temple saying
events.summary: Jesus and his disciples attend a wedding at Cana. The wine runs out, and his mother tells him. He has six stone jars filled with water. The water becomes fine wine, and his disciples believe in him. He goes up to Jerusalem for the Passover. He drives the sellers and money changers out of the temple. He says, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.” He was speaking about his body.
events.detail: The hearers think Jesus means the building (verse 20). Verse 21 says he meant his body. No one understood at the time, including the disciples. Verse 22 says they remembered after he was raised. Then they believed the Scripture and his word. John tells the story from that later point of view. Some sayings can be understood only after the events they point to.

events.title: A teacher's questions stand beside a witness's willingness to decrease
events.summary: Nicodemus, a Pharisee and ruler, comes to Jesus at night. Jesus says no one can see God’s Kingdom without being born anew. Nicodemus asks how that can be. Jesus says God loved the world and gave his only Son. Light has come, and people loved darkness. John’s disciples complain that everyone is going to Jesus. John says he is the bridegroom’s friend and is glad. He says Jesus must increase and he must decrease.
events.detail: John’s disciples are worried about losing their following (verse 26). John answers with a wedding. The bride belongs to the bridegroom (verse 29). The friend stands by and is glad to hear the groom’s voice. John says his joy is complete. Verse 30 then states his place in one line. He was sent to point to another, so growing smaller is success.

events.title: The woman's invitation leads others to hear for themselves
events.summary: Jesus travels through Samaria and rests at Jacob’s well. He asks a Samaritan woman for a drink. He offers her living water and tells her about her life. She asks where people ought to worship. He says true worshipers worship in spirit and truth. She tells her town to come and see. Many Samaritans believe and ask him to stay. In Galilee he heals an official’s son with a word.
events.detail: The woman leaves her water jar and goes to the town (verse 28). She says, “Come, see a man” (verse 29). Many believe because of her word (verse 39). They ask Jesus to stay, and he stays two days. Verse 42 reports what they then tell her. They now believe because they have heard for themselves. Her invitation did its work by bringing them to him.

events.title: The man's lack of help leads into a dispute about work
events.summary: In Jerusalem many sick people lie beside a pool. One man has been ill for thirty-eight years. Jesus asks whether he wants to be well. The man says he has no one to put him in the water. Jesus tells him to take up his mat and walk. It is the Sabbath, and the leaders object. Jesus says his Father is working and he is working. He says the Scriptures testify about him.
events.detail: Jesus asks the man a direct question in verse 6. The man does not say yes. Verse 7 explains why he has not been healed. He has no one to help him into the pool. Others always get there first. He has been alone among a crowd for years. Jesus heals him with a word, and the dispute turns to Sabbath work.

events.summary: Jesus feeds five thousand with five barley loaves and two fish. The crowd wants to make him king, and he withdraws. He walks on the sea to his disciples. The crowd finds him and asks for more bread. He says he is the bread of life that came down from heaven. He speaks of eating his flesh and drinking his blood. Many disciples call this a hard saying and leave. Peter says there is no one else to go to.
events.detail: Verse 60 says many disciples found the teaching hard. Verse 66 says they left and walked with him no more. Jesus asks the twelve whether they will leave too. Peter does not say he understands. Verse 68 asks where else they would go. He stays because of who Jesus is and what he has found in his words. Verse 69 adds that they have come to believe and know.

events.summary: Jesus’s brothers urge him to show himself at the Feast of Booths. He goes up in secret and then teaches in the temple. Some say he is a good man, and others say he deceives the people. Officers are sent to arrest him. On the last day he invites the thirsty to come and drink. The crowd is divided over him. The officers return without him and say no one ever spoke like this. Nicodemus asks whether the law judges a man unheard.
events.detail: This chapter shows a crowd that cannot agree. Verses 12, 40–43 record several opinions at once. The rulers want an arrest and scorn the crowd (verse 49). Nicodemus is one of those rulers. Verse 51 asks a plain legal question. Does their law condemn a man before hearing him? No single response in the chapter speaks for everyone.

events.summary: Jesus says he is the light of the world. The Pharisees say his witness about himself is not valid. He tells those who believed him that the truth will set them free. They answer that they are Abraham’s children and were never slaves. He says everyone who sins is a slave to sin. If they were Abraham’s children, they would do what Abraham did. They are trying to kill him. He says, “Before Abraham came into existence, I AM.”

Verse 40 says they seek to kill a man who told them the truth. He adds, “Abraham didn’t do this.” A family line is shown by family likeness. The words belong to one heated dispute and should not be turned against a people.

events.title: Repeated questioning gives the healed man a voice of his own
events.summary: Jesus sees a man blind from birth. The disciples ask whose sin caused it. He says neither, and he heals the man with mud and washing. Neighbors and Pharisees question the man again and again. His parents are afraid and say he can speak for himself. He says he knows one thing: he was blind and now sees. They throw him out. Jesus finds him, and the man worships him.

Verse 25 refuses to go beyond what he knows. He was blind, and now he sees. He will not call Jesus a sinner to please his judges. By verse 38 he says, “Lord, I believe.”

events.summary: Jesus says the shepherd enters by the door and the sheep know his voice. A thief comes only to steal and kill. Jesus says he is the door and the good shepherd. A hired man runs when the wolf comes. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep. He has other sheep that are not of this fold. At a winter feast some ask whether he is the Christ. He says, “I and the Father are one,” and they pick up stones.

The sheep are not his, and he does not care about them. The test comes when danger arrives. Verse 18 adds that Jesus lays down his life of his own will.

He calls Lazarus out, and the dead man comes out wrapped in cloths. Many believe, and some report it to the Pharisees. The council fears that Rome will destroy their place and nation. The high priest says one man should die for the people.

events.title: The seed image changes the meaning of royal praise
events.summary: Mary anoints Jesus’s feet with costly perfume, and Judas objects. A crowd welcomes Jesus to Jerusalem with palm branches. Some Greeks ask to see him. He says that when he is lifted up he will draw all people to himself. Many still do not believe.
events.detail: The crowd has just hailed Jesus as king (verse 13). Foreigners are asking for him (verse 21). He says the hour of glory has come (verse 23). Verse 24 then explains what that glory is. events.title: The teacher's lowered position supplies the example for followers
events.summary: Before the Passover Jesus rises from supper and ties a towel around himself. He washes his disciples’ feet. Peter objects and then asks to be washed all over. Jesus says they should wash one another’s feet. He is troubled and says one of them will betray him. Judas takes the bread and goes out into the night. Jesus gives a new commandment: love one another as he has loved them. He tells Peter that he will deny him three times.
events.detail: Verse 3 says Jesus knew the Father had given all things into his hands. With that knowledge he takes a servant’s towel. In verse 13 he accepts the titles Teacher and Lord. Verse 14 argues from them. If the Lord has washed their feet, they must wash each other’s. He does not give up his rank to serve. He shows what that rank is for.

events.title: Questions about departure meet a promise of continued teaching
events.summary: Jesus tells his disciples not to be troubled. He is going to prepare a place for them. Thomas says they do not know the way. Jesus says he is the way, the truth, and the life. Philip asks to see the Father. Jesus says whoever has seen him has seen the Father. He promises another Counselor, the Spirit of truth. He leaves them his peace.
events.detail: The disciples ask three anxious questions in this chapter (verses 5, 8, 22). They fear losing him. Verse 26 promises that his teaching will continue. The Holy Spirit will teach them and remind them of his words. The Spirit’s work is tied to what Jesus has already said. Their remembering will be helped. Verse 27 follows with a gift of peace.

events.title: The vine image leads into the command to love
events.summary: Jesus says he is the true vine and his Father is the gardener. Branches that bear fruit are pruned to bear more. A branch cannot bear fruit unless it remains in the vine. His disciples must remain in his love. His commandment is that they love one another as he loved them. He calls them friends and not servants. The world will hate them as it hated him. The Spirit and the disciples will bear witness.
events.detail: Verses 1–8 speak of branches and fruit. Verses 9–10 say that remaining in the vine means remaining in his love. Verse 12 then says what the fruit is. They are to love one another as he has loved them. Verse 13 measures that love by laying down one’s life. Verse 17 repeats the command. The picture of the vine leads straight to it.

events.title: Confidence about understanding meets a warning of scattering
events.summary: Jesus warns that his disciples will be put out of the synagogues. He says it is better for them that he goes away. The Counselor will come and guide them into all truth. They will weep, and their sorrow will turn to joy. He tells them to ask the Father in his name. The disciples say that now they understand and believe. He answers that they will soon be scattered and leave him alone. He tells them to take courage, for he has overcome the world.
events.detail: In verses 29–30 the disciples say they finally understand. They are sure of their belief. Verse 31 answers with a question: “Do you now believe?” Verse 32 says they are about to scatter, each to his own home. They will leave him alone. Their confidence is real and not yet tested. Verse 33 gives them peace that rests on him, not on their firmness.

events.title: The prayer extends belonging beyond the people presently listening
events.summary: Jesus lifts his eyes to heaven and prays. He asks the Father to glorify the Son. He says eternal life is to know the only true God and Jesus Christ. He prays for those the Father gave him. He does not ask that they be taken out of the world. He asks that they be kept from the evil one. He prays also for those who will believe through their word. He asks that they all may be one.
events.detail: Verses 6–19 pray for the disciples in the room. Verse 20 widens the prayer. It includes all who will believe through their word. Later readers are among those prayed for. Verse 21 asks that they all be one, as the Father and Son are one. The purpose is that the world may believe. Verse 15 says they stay in the world for that reason.

events.title: Open testimony contrasts with denial and armed force
events.summary: Jesus goes to a garden across the Kidron, and Judas brings soldiers. Jesus steps forward and says, “I am he.” Peter cuts off a servant’s ear, and Jesus tells him to put away his sword. Jesus is taken to the high priest. Peter denies him three times by a fire. Jesus tells the high priest that he taught openly. He is brought to Pilate, who asks whether he is a king. Jesus says his Kingdom is not of this world.
events.detail: Pilate needs to know whether Jesus is a rival to Rome. Verse 36 answers by pointing to what his followers did not do. If his Kingdom were of this world, they would fight. Jesus stopped the one sword drawn for him (verse 11). His rule does not come by force. He has also said that he spoke openly (verse 20). Peter, meanwhile, denies him in the dark (verses 17, 25–27).

events.title: The execution scene joins completed work with care for those remaining
events.summary: Pilate has Jesus flogged, and soldiers crown him with thorns. Pilate says he finds no guilt and brings him out to the crowd. He hands him over to be crucified. The sign on the cross reads “Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews.” Soldiers divide his clothes. Jesus entrusts his mother to the disciple he loves. He says, “It is finished,” and dies. Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus bury him in a garden tomb.
events.detail: Four soldiers are dividing his clothes (verses 23–24). Near the cross stand his mother and the disciple he loves. Verse 26 gives her a son, and verse 27 gives him a mother. From that hour the disciple takes her into his home. Jesus arranges her care while he is dying. Verse 30 then records, “It is finished.” The finished work includes this act for those left behind.

events.title: Different paths to recognition lead toward readers who have not seen
events.summary: Mary Magdalene finds the tomb open and runs to Peter and another disciple. They see the grave cloths and go home. Mary stays weeping and meets Jesus, whom she takes for the gardener. He says her name, and she knows him. That evening he appears to the disciples behind locked doors. Thomas is absent and says he will not believe without touching the wounds. A week later Jesus invites him to touch. John says he wrote so that readers may believe.
events.detail: People come to recognize Jesus in different ways in this chapter. One disciple sees the cloths and believes (verse 8). Mary knows him when he speaks her name (verse 16). Thomas asks to touch and then confesses him as Lord and God (verse 28). Verse 29 blesses those who have not seen. Verse 31 says the book was written for them. The written signs are offered to readers in place of sight.

events.title: Peter's restored task does not determine another disciple's future
events.summary: Seven disciples go fishing on the Sea of Tiberias and catch nothing. At dawn a man on the shore tells them to cast on the right side. The net fills, and they know it is the Lord. He gives them bread and fish beside a charcoal fire. He asks Peter three times whether he loves him. Each time he tells him to feed his sheep. Peter asks what will happen to another disciple. Jesus says that is not Peter’s concern.
events.detail: Peter denied Jesus three times beside a charcoal fire (18:18). Here he is asked three times beside another (verse 9). He receives a task and word of his own death (verses 18–19). Then he asks about another disciple (verse 21). Jesus says that is not Peter’s concern and tells him to follow. Verse 23 corrects a rumor that grew from this. Jesus said “if,” and people heard a promise.

words.label: Levites
words.meaning: Members of the tribe of Levi. They cared for the tabernacle and later the temple. The priests came from one Levite family, Aaron’s.

words.label: Sabbath
words.meaning: The seventh day of the week, kept as a day of rest.

words.label: Pharisees
words.meaning: A Jewish group known for careful keeping of the law. Acts 23:8 says they believed in resurrection, angels, and spirits.

words.label: Scribes
words.meaning: People trained to write and to keep records. In the Gospels, scribes also teach the law.

words.label: Synagogue
words.meaning: A local Jewish meeting place for prayer and for reading Scripture.

words.label: Passover
words.meaning: A yearly feast that recalls Israel’s escape from Egypt. Exodus 12 gives its first account.

words.label: Circumcision
words.meaning: The cutting of the foreskin. Genesis 17 makes it the sign of God’s covenant with Abraham.

words.label: Manna
words.meaning: The food Israel gathered in the wilderness. Exodus 16 describes it.

words.label: Anoint
words.meaning: To pour oil on a person or thing to set it apart. Kings and priests were anointed.

words.label: Messiah
words.meaning: The Hebrew title “anointed one.” John 1:41 gives “Christ” as the same title in Greek.

words.label: Zion
words.meaning: A hill in Jerusalem. The name is also used for the city and its people.

words.label: Samaritans
words.meaning: People of Samaria, between Judea and Galilee. John 4:9 says Jews had no dealings with them.

words.label: Rabbi
words.meaning: A title of respect for a teacher. John 1:38 gives the meaning as “Teacher.”

words.label: Parable
words.meaning: A short story or comparison that teaches a point.

words.label: Cubit
words.meaning: A length from the elbow to the fingertip, about 46 centimeters.

words.label: Denarius
words.meaning: A Roman silver coin. Matthew 20:2 gives it as a worker’s pay for one day.

chapterMaps.narrative: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God and was God. All things were made through him. The Word became flesh and lived among us. John the Baptist says he is not the Christ. He points to Jesus as the Lamb of God. Two of John’s disciples follow Jesus and spend the day with him. Andrew brings his brother Simon. Philip brings Nathanael, who doubts that anything good comes from Nazareth.

Peter asks what will happen to another disciple. Jesus says that is not Peter’s concern.
